newsitem.title: USA: U.N. chief swipes at Clinton on land mine policy.
newsitem.headline: U.N. chief swipes at Clinton on land mine policy.

text.p: United Nations Secretary-General Kofi Annan urged all governments on Wednesday to swiftly ban the use, production and stockpiling of anti-personnel landmines.

In what amounted to a swipe at President Bill Clinton's landmine policy, Annan, a former U.N. undersecretary for peacekeeping operations, strongly backed a Canadian-led, "fast-track" approach to banning "these abominable weapons."

The Clinton administration, reluctant to foreswear a weapon before China and Russia do likewise, has refused to join the Canadian drive. Instead, the Pentagon favours a worldwide ban through the U.N. Conference on Disarmament that experts say could take a decade or more to negotiate.

"I don't think we need to wait for others to do the right thing," Annan told an audience at the Heritage Foundation, a private research group. "I don't think governments need to wait for anyone to say that we're going to abolish these abominable weapons.

"I therefore support the Ottawa approach and hope that as many countries as possible will join it," Annan added. The Canadian proposal, which is also backed by most of the United States Senate, calls for all willing countries to sign a treaty in Ottawa in December.

The Canadian-proposed treaty would ban the use, production and stockpiling of mines by the year 2000. At least 58 U.S. senators have voiced support of a similar measure, though they would let the Pentagon continue to deploy mines in the demilitarized zone between North and South Korea.
Anti-personnel landmines, planted during war and often forgotten when fighting ends, kill or maim 2,000 people every month, often civilians, according to the American Red Cross.

Pressed on what he would tell Clinton about the United States refusal to join the Ottawa process, Annan said: I think my answer is clear -- that I would encourage governments to do it as quickly as they can, without waiting for others to do it."
The Pentagon said on Tuesday that Russia had made it clear it was not willing to participate in the so-called Ottawa process. It said China had not yet made a decision.

"We just believe that there needs to be an all-inclusive approach to this thing, which can only be accomplished through the Conference on Disarmament," a Pentagon spokesman, Navy Capt. Michael Doubleday, said.
Annan said that ultimately the Disarmament Conference approach would merge with any treaty signed in Ottawa.
"The disarmament conference...will bring everybody in under the same umbrella, but the more governments we get that agree to ban the weapons now, the better we are," he said.
